AUTOMATED,
COST-EFFICIENT
HAR-
NESS EVOLUTION FOR GENERALIZATION TO UNSEEN
TASKS
Euntae Choi∗
Seoul National University
euntae.choi175@gmail.com
Sumin Song∗
Seoul National University
songsm921@snu.ac.kr
Sungjoo Yoo†

ABSTRACT
An LLM agent is defined by two things: the weights inside its model and the
harness of components assembled around it. Harnesses are still handcrafted, and
HarnessX, which evolves them automatically, starts each benchmark from a hand-
crafted harness, reports gains on the tasks it evolved on, and budgets 100 to 175
million meta-agent tokens per benchmark. We propose LiteEvo, a lightweight
harness-evolution algorithm whose tool-free meta-agents mine agent trajectories
for reusable components, curate them into a versioned library, and compose each
round’s harness from it, starting every benchmark from the same neutral harness
and never naming the benchmark. Evolving on the graded tasks of five agentic
benchmarks with a frozen Qwen3.5-9B, LiteEvo lifts pass@2 by 10.5 to 67.7 pp
and reaches comparable or higher pass@2 than a reproduction of HarnessX (71.0
against 67.3 on average) at 13.0× lower mean API cost. Harnesses evolved on
train tasks keep their gains on unseen test tasks of four benchmarks, and LiteEvo
also lifts Claude Code with Sonnet 4.6 by 1.2 to 71.4 pp.
1
INTRODUCTION
Every language-model agent runs inside a harness, the layer that turns the model’s replies into
actions and the environment’s responses into its next input. Its prompt, action and observation pro-
cessing, and loop settings can decide whether a task is solved: given only the task text, a frozen
Qwen3.5-9B solves none of AppWorld’s test tasks, but with a harness that LiteEvo evolves on sep-
arate training tasks, the same model solves 65.5% of them within two attempts (Table 1). Changing
the harness needs no gradient step and applies to closed models as well, whereas training the weights
of a coding agent with reinforcement learning takes 512 GPUs for about 32 hours (Wei et al., 2025a).
Recent work automates harness design with a frontier model that acts as a meta-agent, reading
the agent’s traces and rewriting its harness (Chen et al., 2026; Lee et al., 2026; Lou et al., 2026).
HarnessX (Chen et al., 2026) applies this idea to five agentic benchmarks, but at a high price, with a
budget of 100 to 175 million meta-agent tokens per benchmark, and with human knowledge built in:
it starts each benchmark from a handcrafted harness, so every new environment needs new human
effort, and the gains it reports mix what evolution found with what the seed already knew. Its paper
also reports gains at the best round on the tasks it evolved on and does not test whether an evolved
harness helps on tasks it has not seen.
Other systems share some of these limits. Methods in which a model designs agents automatically
report search costs of hundreds to tens of thousands of dollars per run (Hu et al., 2025; Robeyns et al.,
2025; Zhang et al., 2026c), and each of the closest harness-evolution methods tells its optimizer

about the benchmark in some form (Table 6): Meta-Harness (Lee et al., 2026) guides its proposer
with a hand-written skill for each domain, AutoHarness (Lou et al., 2026) gives its refiner the game’s
name and description, and HarnessCompass (Zhang et al., 2026d) puts software-repair hints into its
meta prompt. Three recent methods start from a minimal harness or score on held-out tasks, but each
covers at most two of our five benchmarks (Zhang et al., 2026d;b; Yang et al., 2026). It therefore
remains open whether a cheap evolution loop that knows nothing about the benchmark, neither
through its starting harness nor through its instructions, can produce harnesses that help on unseen
tasks across agentic benchmarks as different as ours.
We address this question with LiteEvo, a harness-evolution loop designed for low API cost and
a benchmark-blind start. Every benchmark starts from the same neutral harness, a 788-character
description of the turn protocol with no benchmark-specific content, and the four meta-agents are
never told which benchmark they work on: a filter masks names and identifiers in everything they
read, and their instructions forbid using recalled knowledge of a benchmark. Apart from this harness
and the benchmark interfaces, the only parts we design by hand are the loop and the meta-agents’
instructions, so the benchmark-specific content of a returned harness is learned from the agent’s own
trajectories. In each round, a single analyst reads a failure-oriented sample of these trajectories: the
tasks that some attempts solve and others fail, and the lowest-scoring tasks that no attempt solves.
Three more meta-agents turn its diagnosis into edits of a versioned component library and a new
harness, for about five tool-free API calls per round in all; a pass@2 gate then decides whether
to keep that harness (Figure 2). We evaluate LiteEvo both transductively, as HarnessX does, and
inductively, on test tasks the loop never sees. Our contributions are as follows:
• LiteEvo, a generic harness-evolution method that needs no benchmark-specific seed: it
starts every benchmark from the same neutral harness, never tells its four tool-free meta-
agents which benchmark they work on, and evolves the harness through failure-oriented
group sampling, a versioned library of typed components and a pass@2 gate.
• Comparable or higher pass@2 for a small share of the API cost: with a frozen Qwen3.5-9B
on ALFWorld, WebShop, AppWorld, GAIA and SWE-bench Verified, LiteEvo reaches a
mean pass@2 of 71.0 against 67.3 for a same-stack reproduction of HarnessX when both
evolve on the graded tasks, at a 13.0× lower mean API cost (Figure 1).

Figure 2: Overview of LiteEvo. (0) Every benchmark starts from the same neutral harness h0.
(1) Frozen workers run the current harness ht on the train tasks, and failure-oriented group sampling
keeps ten mixed-outcome and three all-fail task groups as evidence. (2) Four meta-agents mine fail-
ure modes, curate a versioned component library († marks the strategies, which advise the composer
and never reach the agent) and compose a candidate. (3) A pass@2 gate on the val tasks accepts,
holds or reverts the candidate. (4) The frozen agent runs the selected harness ht+1 in the next round.
• Generalization beyond the evolution tasks: harnesses that LiteEvo evolves on train tasks
and selects on val tasks stay within 2.2 pp of the transductive ones on unseen test tasks
of ALFWorld and AppWorld, exceed them on WebShop and SWE-bench Verified (70.0
against 62.7 and 66.7 against 63.2), and reach 48.6 pass@2 on AppWorld tasks that need
apps unseen in training, where the neutral harness solves none; transfer to an unseen bench-
mark remains open.
2
PRELIMINARIES
Tasks and the Frozen Agent.
A benchmark provides a set of tasks T , each an interactive environ-
ment whose first observation states the task and which answers every action with a new observation.
When an episode ends, the benchmark’s own evaluator returns a success flag y ∈{0, 1} and a partial
credit f ∈[0, 1]. The agent, a frozen language model with fixed decoding, acts through a fixed run-
ner: a multi-turn chat loop that passes the action in each reply to the environment until the episode
ends or a per-benchmark turn cap is reached.
Harness.
A harness h = (p, Φ, κ) is everything that may change between the frozen model and
the environment. Here p is the system prompt, and Φ is a set of processors, short programs that
the runner calls at fixed points of a turn. A processor can add a one-turn message before the model
call, rewrite the action after it is extracted, or rewrite the observation after the environment step.
The last part, κ, sets five runner knobs, which control the reply protocol, the listing of available
actions, an observation length cap, a last-line action fallback and a display of the remaining turns.
The environment, the turn cap, the decoding parameters and the model lie outside the harness and
never change.

Metric and Regimes.
We measure a harness by pass@k(h; T ), the probability that at least one
of k independent attempts at a task succeeds, averaged over a task set T and estimated with the
unbiased estimator of Chen et al. (2021). The tasks fall into three sets: (i) train tasks Ttrain, whose
trajectories a method may read, (ii) val tasks Tval, used to choose between harnesses, and (iii) test
tasks Ttest, used to grade the harness a method returns. The inductive regime keeps the three sets
disjoint, so that the test tasks stay unseen during evolution, whereas the transductive regime uses
one task set for all three, as HarnessX does for all its results (Chen et al., 2026). As a floor, the bare
agent receives only the benchmark’s own task text, with no system prompt.
3
LITEEVO
LiteEvo is a fully automated harness-evolution algorithm: given a frozen agent and a benchmark,
it improves the agent’s harness over R rounds, starting from a neutral harness h0 that is the same
for every benchmark and using no human input written for the benchmark (Figure 2, Algorithm 1).
Round t runs the current harness ht with M frozen workers on the train tasks. Four meta-agents
then turn the resulting trajectories into a candidate hcand: the analyst diagnoses failure modes and
proposes components, the editor selects and checks them, the librarian records them in a versioned
library L of components, and the composer assembles the candidate from L, while a journal J
keeps each round’s scores, decisions and failure modes for later rounds. A pass@2 gate on the val
tasks then compares the candidate’s score st with the score b⋆of the best harness so far, h⋆, and
picks the harness ht+1 of the next round, either hcand or h⋆. Round 0 thus runs the neutral harness,
and each of the R −1 evolution rounds that follow runs the harness that the gate picked in the round
before. In the inductive regime the train and val rollouts come from disjoint task sets, whereas in the
transductive regime both come from the test tasks and the gate reuses the train rollouts.
The meta-agents read what the agent did and how its episodes ended but never act in an environment:
each of their calls is a single request without tools that returns structured output. Apart from h0 and
the runner that connects the agent to each benchmark, the only parts we design by hand are the loop
and the meta-agents’ instructions, neither of which names or describes any specific benchmark;
Appendix B lists all human inputs.
3.1
A NEUTRAL START AND BENCHMARK-BLIND META-AGENTS
LiteEvo starts all five benchmarks from one neutral harness h0, whose 788-character prompt p
states only the protocol of an episode: the agent reads an observation, replies with one action inside
4


--- Page 5 ---
Preprint
action tags, and has a limited number of turns. Where actions are code, the reply format allows a
multi-line action. Since h0 has no processors and uses default knob values, what a returned harness
knows about its benchmark comes from evolution, apart from generic advice in the meta-agents’
instructions. HarnessX, by contrast, starts each benchmark from a handcrafted harness (Chen et al.,
2026); its GAIA prompt alone holds about 11,000 characters of hand-written search recipes, several
of which name specific websites.
The meta-agents are blind to the benchmark as well. Before a meta-agent reads a trajectory, a filter
removes task identifiers, split names and URLs, masks benchmark and dataset names, and shows
the turn limit only as short or long, a label that at least two benchmarks share. The meta-agents’
instructions forbid relying on recalled knowledge of a benchmark, even if they recognize it, and
Appendix B details how both rules are enforced.
3.2
FAILURE-ORIENTED GROUP SAMPLING
Each round evaluates the current harness with M frozen workers, each of which runs ht once on
every train task, so that every task yields M trajectories that form its group. The groups are the
input of the analyst, the first meta-agent, but it does not read all of them. A group is mixed when
some but not all workers solve the task, and all-fail when none does; with failure-oriented group
sampling, the analyst reads the ten mixed groups with the highest mean partial credit and the three
all-fail groups with the lowest. Each comes with all M trajectories and their outcomes, together
with outcome statistics over the whole round and the prompt p that the agent ran (Algorithm 2). The
two kinds serve different ends. A success and a failure in one mixed group share the task and the
harness and differ only by sampling, so the step that separates them is one that the harness leaves to
chance, and fixing it makes the harness more reliable (exploitation). An all-fail group instead shows
a task that the harness does not yet make solvable, and asks for the insight that would (exploration).
Without both kinds, evolution stalls where successes are rare and hard to reach, as on AppWorld:
reading only all-success or only all-fail groups ends there at 16.9 and 12.3 pass@2, against 67.7
with both (Appendix D.6). The design echoes group-relative reinforcement learning, which learns
only from groups whose rewards differ (Shao et al., 2024; Yu et al., 2025), and Training-Free GRPO,
which turns such within-group contrasts into prompt-level experience (Cai et al., 2025); unlike them,
LiteEvo also keeps all-fail groups, as targets for exploration.
3.3
THE META-AGENT STAGE
The library L stores typed components that fill the three parts of a harness h = (p, Φ, κ). Prompt
fragments, which are instructions or worked examples, and knowledge components, which record
facts about the environment seen in trajectories, go into the prompt p; processors go into Φ, and knob
components hold settings for κ. A fifth kind, strategies, advises the composer and never reaches the
agent. Initially the library is empty except for three hand-written strategies, generic composing
rules such as leaving the reply format to the runner (Appendix B). The edits of a round produce a
new library version, and components record when they were selected and how often they fired. On
AppWorld, for instance, the returned harness holds a worked login example as a fragment and the
login API’s credential fields as knowledge, and one of its processors restates the login steps after
two authorization errors.
Analyst.
The analyst first compares the trajectories within each sampled group and only then
generalizes across groups. It returns a list of failure modes, giving for each one its share of the
failures, the evidence and the mechanism behind it. For each mode, it also proposes candidate
components of a given kind, written out in full. Its instructions ask for fixes that the harness can
carry out, such as a worked example or a processor, rather than general advice to the agent.
Editor.
The editor merges, rewrites or drops the analyst’s candidates with a reason for each deci-
sion, reading a journal J of earlier rounds (their gate scores, decisions, failure modes and rejected
components) so that it does not repeat a change that already failed. Every processor it keeps is com-
piled and replayed on 24 episodes of the round, and one that does not compile, raises an error or
never fires is dropped; a separate review call then reads the outputs of each remaining processor and
drops those that contradict its stated purpose.
5


--- Page 6 ---
Preprint
Librarian.
The librarian applies the editor’s selection to the library: it sees all components with
their usage statistics and returns operations that add a component, update or merge existing ones, or
drop one. Each operation is validated again before it is applied: a processor must compile, a knob
setting must parse, and no body may name a benchmark. The library is never rolled back, and a
component therefore survives even when the harness that first used it is reverted.
Composer.
The composer writes the candidate harness from the library: it selects components,
writes a free-text frame that opens the prompt, and sets the five knobs. It sees the library’s index and
bodies, the journal, the selection and knobs of the best harness h⋆, the editor’s picks, and a short
excerpt of failed trajectories. A fixed assembly then builds hcand = (p, Φ, κ): p joins the frame,
the selected prompt fragments and knowledge, and the runner’s reply-format block; Φ holds the
selected processors; and κ takes the composer’s knob values. The composer builds each candidate
afresh from the library instead of editing the previous harness.
3.4
THE PASS@2 GATE
The gate keeps the best harness so far, h⋆, and its val score b⋆, initially h0 and its own score. It
scores a candidate by st = pass@2(hcand; Tval), the metric we report, estimated from M rollouts
per val task, and picks the harness of the next round:
ht+1 =



hcand, and (h⋆, b⋆) ←(hcand, st)
if st > b⋆
(accept),
h⋆
if st < b⋆−δ
(revert),
hcand
otherwise
(hold).
(1)
A hold keeps searching from the candidate without making it the best harness. The margin δ is the
largest of three quantities (Appendix B): (i) 7 pp, or half of b⋆if that is smaller, (ii) a noise band
estimated from how far the workers’ scores spread within the rounds so far, and (iii) the spread of
the best harness’s repeated measurements. A candidate whose replies fail to parse more than 5% of
the time is never accepted. After R rounds, LiteEvo returns h⋆, and a result’s best round t means
that the returned harness is ht, first run in round t. In the loop itself, a candidate’s val rollouts run at
the start of the next round together with its train rollouts, so the meta-agents have already composed
from them when the gate decides; a revert discards that composition, while the library keeps its
edits.
3.5
WHY LITEEVO IS CHEAP
Three design choices keep the API cost of LiteEvo low. First, every meta-agent call is a single
tool-free request on an input that the loop assembles, so that a round makes about five calls, one per
meta-agent plus the editor’s processor review, which Figure 2 and Algorithm 1 omit for brevity. An
agentic meta-agent such as HarnessX’s instead works through dozens of tool-using turns per round
and re-sends its growing context at each of them (Chen et al., 2026). Second, only the analyst reads
full trajectories, and only a fixed-size sample of them, on the cheaper of the two models, while the
other meta-agents read far shorter inputs, such as its structured output, the journal and the library.
Third, the library persists across rounds, so that a round adds or revises a few components instead
of re-deriving the harness from the trajectories. Section 4 measures the resulting cost.
4
EVALUATION
4.1
EXPERIMENTAL SETUP
Models and Benchmarks.
We evaluate on ALFWorld (Shridhar et al., 2021), WebShop (Yao
et al., 2022), AppWorld (Trivedi et al., 2024), GAIA (Mialon et al., 2024) and SWE-bench Veri-
fied (Jimenez et al., 2024), which ask for household tasks in a text world, product searches, every-
day tasks through the APIs of nine apps, web research with code, and repository-level bug fixes.
The frozen agent is Qwen3.5-9B in thinking mode, served locally, and the analyst runs on Claude
Sonnet 5 and the other three meta-agents on Claude Opus 4.6.

Implementation Details.
Each run lasts R = 8 rounds, round 0 with the neutral harness and seven
evolution rounds, with M = 4 workers (M = 2 on SWE-bench Verified). Unless a caption says
otherwise, we grade a returned harness in three test runs of two attempts per task and report the
mean pass@1 and pass@2. The API cost of a run counts the meta-agents’ tokens in the calls that
produce h1 to h7, at Opus 4.6’s list price and Sonnet 5’s introductory price. We leave out the cost of
running the agent, which runs on local GPUs, for all methods: every harness-evolution method pays
it, and comparing it fairly would need one common setup for running the agent, which was not yet
fully reproducible at the time of submission.
Baselines.
We compare with the bare agent and with HarnessX (Chen et al., 2026), which we re-
produce from its released code with the same agent and tasks, using Opus 4.6 as its meta-agent for
eight rounds. As in its paper, HarnessX evolves on the tasks it is graded on, and we report its best
round; we wrote its seeds for ALFWorld, WebShop and AppWorld, which the release lacks. On
GAIA, whose agent searches the live web, LiteEvo’s web tools block known copies of the bench-
mark’s answers. For details of the setup not mentioned here, see Appendix C.
4.2
MAIN RESULTS
Main Comparison.
Table 1 compares LiteEvo with HarnessX, and Figure 1a plots each run’s
pass@2 against its API cost. In the transductive regime, where both methods evolve on the tasks
they are graded on, LiteEvo reaches a mean pass@2 of 71.0 over the five benchmarks, compared with
67.3 for HarnessX. It spends $8.24 to $24.30 per run where HarnessX spends $118.47 to $190.32,
a 13.0× lower mean API cost. It does so from a weaker start on all five benchmarks: the neutral

harness solves no AppWorld task, whereas the handcrafted seed reaches 48.6, and it scores 10.0 on
WebShop, where the seed reaches 45.3. Evolution closes both gaps within eight rounds, adding 67.7
and 52.7 pp of pass@2. The neutral harness is not always the strongest trivial start: the bare agent
scores 24.0 on WebShop, and a one-line format hint reaches 61.2 on SWE-bench Verified (Table 2).
Measured from these stronger starts, LiteEvo’s transductive gains are 38.7 and 2.0 pp.
Cost Breakdown.
As Section 3.5 anticipates, HarnessX’s meta-agent, an agentic session with file
tools, makes 65 to 130 Opus calls and consumes 3.3 to 5.6 million input tokens per round in our
reproduction, whereas LiteEvo makes about five calls and consumes 0.12 to 0.54 million, mostly
read by the analyst on the cheaper Sonnet 5.
Inductive Transfer.
The inductive runs of Table 1 evolve on train tasks, choose between harnesses
on val tasks, and are graded on test tasks that the loop never sees. On ALFWorld and AppWorld
they stay within 2.2 pp of the transductive runs, and on WebShop and SWE-bench Verified they
score higher, with 70.0 against 62.7 and 66.7 against 63.2; the inductive harnesses also score above
HarnessX’s transductive ones, although HarnessX, which reports no held-out evaluation, selected
its harnesses on the test tasks themselves. GAIA has no inductive row, as its 103 public questions
are too few to split three ways. On AppWorld tasks that need apps unseen in training, our inductive
harness reaches 48.6 where the neutral harness solves none, against 49.2 for our transductive one
and 50.5 for HarnessX’s (Appendix D.2); a library evolved on other benchmarks does not yet help
an unseen one.

Other Backbones.
Table 3 applies LiteEvo to Claude Code (Anthropic, 2026a) running Son-
net 4.6: the composed system prompt is appended to Claude Code’s own, and the processors act
on the actions and observations exchanged with the environment. LiteEvo raises pass@2 in all nine
benchmark and regime cells at $8.21 to $12.92 per run: by 1.2 to 7.5 pp on the four benchmarks
where the bare agent is already strong, and on AppWorld from 0.0 to 66.1 in the transductive regime
and to 71.4 in the inductive one. On the smaller Qwen3.5-4B, LiteEvo adds 6.7 to 49.8 pp to the
neutral start (Appendix D.1).
4.3
ABLATION STUDIES
This section examines how the returned harness splits between its prompt and its processors, how
the library grows, and whether a handcrafted start helps; for more ablations, see Appendix D.
Prompt versus Processors.
Table 2 splits a returned harness into its system prompt and its pro-
cessors. The full harness gives the best pass@2 on all five benchmarks. The prompt carries most of
the gain on ALFWorld and AppWorld, reaching 95.5 and 63.1 alone compared with 96.3 and 67.7
for the full harness; on GAIA and SWE-bench Verified the processors do, reaching 59.2 and 63.1
alone compared with 65.2 and 63.2. Since the two parts evolved together, the split does not isolate
their contributions.
Library Growth.
In the five transductive runs (Table 4), the librarian mostly adds, with 85 addi-
tions against 25 updates, 7 merges and 2 drops, so the library grows from 3.8 components on average
after the first round to 16.4 after the last. The composer uses all components in the first two rounds
and then becomes selective, picking 75.6% of them in the last round. Forcing an explicit memory
across episodes into every harness lowered pass@2 (Appendix D.8).
Neutral versus Handcrafted Start.
Table 5 starts LiteEvo from a handcrafted HarnessX-style
seed instead of the neutral harness. The seeded runs end lower on both benchmarks, with 64.9
against 67.7 on AppWorld and 59.9 against 65.2 on GAIA, so the neutral start matches or exceeds a
handcrafted one and is our default; with one run per arm, this does not show that a seed hurts.
9


--- Page 10 ---
Preprint
5
CONCLUSION
We introduced LiteEvo, which evolves a harness from the same neutral start on every benchmark
with four tool-free meta-agents, a versioned component library and a pass@2 gate. With a frozen
Qwen3.5-9B, it reaches comparable or higher pass@2 than our reproduction of HarnessX (71.0
against 67.3 on average) at 13.0× lower mean API cost, from one run per benchmark. Its inductive
harnesses keep their gains on unseen test tasks, and a handcrafted seed did not improve on the neutral
start (Appendix E discusses limitations and future work).
AI USE STATEMENT
We used generative AI tools heavily to polish the manuscript and to correct non-native English
expressions. For the appendix, AI agents also drafted text, which we read and verified. We developed
the meta-agents’ instructions with the help of AI agents, but we verified sensitive content by hand, in
particular that no instruction leaks information about a benchmark. AI agents also ran and monitored
our experiments, while we verified the reported results and the evaluation code ourselves. We wrote
the instructions for the supplementary code with an AI agent and ran the code on our own server to
confirm that it works. Apart from these uses, LiteEvo itself runs on LLMs: the agent and all four
meta-agents are language models, as Sections 2 and 3 describe. We take responsibility for the final
content of this work, including text, claims or artifacts produced with the aid of generative AI.
ETHICS STATEMENT
This work evaluates agents on public benchmarks inside sandboxed environments and involves no
human subjects. Agents that search the web can reach published copies of benchmark answers.
Appendix C.4 describes how we block known copies on GAIA and what exposure remains.
REPRODUCIBILITY STATEMENT
Section 3 and Appendix B specify the loop, the meta-agents, the gate and every setting, and Ap-
pendix B.1 gives the neutral harness verbatim. Appendix C gives the task sets, the grading protocol,
the cost accounting and the HarnessX reproduction. As supplementary material, we attach a mini-
mal set of our code that runs the LiteEvo experiments. We will release the full code on GitHub upon
acceptance.

A
RELATED WORK
HarnessX (Chen et al., 2026) is the closest work: its Opus 4.6 meta-agent evolves harnesses on four
of our five benchmarks, starting each from a handcrafted harness, and the paper reports peak-round
pass@2 on the tasks it evolves on. Other harness optimizers likewise build knowledge of the bench-
mark into the start or into the optimizer’s instructions, through per-domain seeds and skills (Lee
et al., 2026), the benchmark’s official agent (Zhang et al., 2026e), the game’s description (Lou
et al., 2026), an exploration agent aimed at the benchmark (Lin et al., 2026a), or software-repair
hints (Zhang et al., 2026d). Methods that evolve whole agents report high costs for a whole run:
about $300 to $500 for ADAS, which scores held-out tasks, and about $7,000 and $22,000 for the
self-improving coding agents SICA and DGM (Hu et al., 2025; Robeyns et al., 2025; Zhang et al.,
2026c). Cheaper methods that score held-out tasks, such as GEPA and Better Harnesses, are evalu-
ated on none of our benchmarks (Agrawal et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026). Once search and test tasks
are separated, harness evolution in the style of AHE gains only 0.6 pp on Terminal-Bench 2.1 (Wang
et al., 2026). LiteEvo targets all of these limits at once: it starts all five benchmarks from one neutral
harness, never names the benchmark to its meta-agents, costs under $30 per run in API calls, and
reports held-out as well as transductive scores.
Table 6 compares LiteEvo with the closest methods on four axes: the starting harness, what the
optimizer is told about the benchmark, how far from the evolution tasks the result is measured, and
the optimizer cost that each paper reports.
Table 6: How LiteEvo and the closest methods start, what their optimizer is told about the bench-
mark, how far from the evolution tasks they are evaluated, and what optimizer cost they report.
Levels: L0, evolved and graded on the same tasks; L1, unseen tasks of the same benchmark; L1.5,
tasks that need unseen apps; L2, a sibling benchmark; L3, a foreign benchmark. Evo-Bench is a
benchmark of evolver models rather than a method.

Training the Agent’s Weights.
Reinforcement learning trains an agent’s weights on its own multi-
turn interaction (Feng et al., 2025; Dong et al., 2026; Xi et al., 2026; Wei et al., 2025b); Zhang et al.
(2026a) survey the area. Such training adapts the model itself, but one run occupies a GPU cluster:
SWE-RL trains on 512 GPUs for about 32 hours (Wei et al., 2025a), and DeepSWE on 64 GPUs
for six days (Luo et al., 2025). Supervised fine-tuning on agent trajectories (Zeng et al., 2024; Chen
et al., 2023; Song et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2024b) is cheaper per run but needs trajectories from a
17


--- Page 18 ---
Preprint
stronger model, and it applies only to open weights. Since LiteEvo changes no weight, it applies to
closed agents such as Claude Code, and its evolved harnesses could be combined with either kind of
training.
Multi-Agent Orchestration.
Multi-agent systems split a task among specialist agents under an
orchestrator or a fixed workflow (Wu et al., 2024; Hong et al., 2024; Fourney et al., 2024; Nielsen
et al., 2026). LiteEvo uses several LLM roles as well, but only offline, to write the harness of a
single agent that then runs alone at test time.
How Much the Harness Matters.
With the model fixed, scores vary widely with the harness:
SWE-agent’s interface solves 10.7 pp more SWE-bench instances than a plain shell with the same
model (Yang et al., 2024b). A coding agent that the DGM evolved lifts Claude 3.7 Sonnet from
19.0% to 59.5% on 200 SWE-bench tasks (Zhang et al., 2026c), and one model scores from 13.9%
to 37.6% on Terminal-Bench 2 depending on its harness (Lee et al., 2026). Coding agents such as
Claude Code are themselves harnesses around a model (Anthropic, 2026b; Wang et al., 2025a). The
choice of model can still matter more than the harness (Merrill et al., 2026), which is one reason we
also evolve harnesses for a frontier agent (Table 3).
Prompt, Context and Memory Optimization.
Prompt optimizers tune the instructions and
demonstrations of a fixed program from feedback (Khattab et al., 2024; Opsahl-Ong et al., 2024;
Yang et al., 2024a; Yuksekgonul et al., 2024). GEPA reflects on traces to evolve prompts and beats
reinforcement learning with up to 35× fewer rollouts (Agrawal et al., 2026), and ACE grows a play-
book of strategies in an agent’s context (Zhang et al., 2026e). A second line keeps experience in
memory: Reflexion retries a task with verbal self-reflection (Shinn et al., 2023), ExpeL and Au-
toManual distill insights or manuals from training tasks (Zhao et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2024a), and
Agent Workflow Memory, Dynamic Cheatsheet and ReasoningBank accumulate workflows, notes
or strategies as a test stream unfolds (Wang et al., 2025b; Suzgun et al., 2026; Ouyang et al., 2026).
LiteEvo’s library stores the same kinds of knowledge in typed components, next to processors and
runner settings, and a composer decides which of them the agent sees. Unlike test-stream memories,
LiteEvo fits its library offline and freezes its harness at test time.
Automated Design of Agents and Harnesses.
Earlier work searches over whole agent designs:
ADAS programs new agents in code (Hu et al., 2025), AFlow searches over code-represented work-
flows (Zhang et al., 2025b), AgentSquare searches a modular design space (Shang et al., 2025),
and MaAS samples multi-agent systems from a learned supernet (Zhang et al., 2025a). DGM and
SICA let a coding agent rewrite its own code, at about $22,000 and $7,000 per run (Zhang et al.,
2026c; Robeyns et al., 2025). Harness evolution instead keeps the model fixed and changes the layer
around it. HarnessX, Meta-Harness, AutoHarness, AHE, HarnessCompass and Self-Harness evolve
prompts, tools and code around a task agent (Chen et al., 2026; Lee et al., 2026; Lou et al., 2026; Lin
et al., 2026a; Zhang et al., 2026d;b), several of them with agentic meta-agents that use file or web
tools. Better Harnesses fits harnesses for small models at $20 per run, rollouts included (Yang et al.,
2026). Studies of the setting find that gains shrink when search and test are separated (Wang et al.,
2026) and that a small evolver can match a frontier one on in-place skill edits (Lin et al., 2026b),
while Evo-Bench evaluates evolvers on held-out tasks (Huang et al., 2026). LiteEvo’s meta-agents,
by contrast, are tool-free, read a failure-oriented sample of trajectories instead of full traces, and
never see the benchmark’s name.

--- Page 19 ---

B
METHOD DETAILS
This appendix gives what Section 3 and Algorithm 1 leave out.
B.1
THE NEUTRAL HARNESS
Every run starts from the system prompt in Figure 3, which is 788 characters long and, with the
runner’s reply-format block, labels and reminder (Appendix B.9), is the only text we write for the
agent.
Neutral Harness (𝒉𝟎)
You are an autonomous agent operating in a text environment over a
sequence of turns.
Each turn you receive an observation describing the current state. You
reply with exactly one action. The environment then returns the next
observation.
Reply format -- put your action inside action tags:
<action>the action, written exactly as the environment expects</action>
The environment alone defines which actions exist and how they must be
written. Read each observation carefully: it is your only source of truth
about what is available and about what your last action did. Anything you
write outside the action tags is not sent to the environment.
You have a limited number of turns. The episode ends when the environment
reports that it is finished, or when the turn budget is exhausted.
Figure 3: The neutral harness h0, the system prompt with which every run starts. Line breaks inside
paragraphs are added for display.
On AppWorld, GAIA and SWE-bench Verified, whose actions are code, the text changes in three
places and grows to 977 characters: “one action” becomes “one action block”, the example spans
two lines, and one sentence says that the text inside the tags may span several lines and runs as one
unit. The neutral harness has no processors, and its knobs take the defaults of Table 7.
B.2
THE RUNNER
The runner is a multi-turn chat loop, the same for all benchmarks and harnesses. Its system message
is s, and each user message holds the latest observation, preceded by the number of turns left and
followed by the list of available actions when the knobs ask for them. The model thinks before it
replies, but its reasoning is not kept in the history. The system message and the first observation
are never dropped; past a prompt budget of 32,768 tokens, the oldest reply–observation pairs are
dropped, while the four most recent are always kept. The runner executes the text inside the first
<action> tag of a reply, or the rest of the reply if the tag is never closed. On ALFWorld and
WebShop it can fall back to the reply’s last line; no other text reaches the environment. A reply
without an action gets a fixed one-sentence reminder, and on the benchmarks whose actions are
code, the first three such replies of an episode do not use up a turn.
19


--- Page 20 ---
Preprint
B.3
PROCESSORS AND KNOBS
A processor is a Python function advise(ctx) that returns a dictionary. Its context exposes the
turn index and budget, the task, the last observation and action, the available actions, the steps taken
so far, and a scratchpad shared by the processors of one episode, but never the model’s reasoning or
the reply being processed. Each hook accepts one key:
• before model may return inject, a message that only the next model call sees;
• after model may return rewrite action, which replaces the extracted action;
• after step may return rewrite obs, which replaces the observation the model reads.
The trajectory record that the analyst reads keeps the environment’s original text.
Processors on one hook run in a fixed order, each with an allow-listed set of built-ins and the modules
re and json but no imports, and an exception inside a processor is caught and counts as an empty
return. Table 7 lists the five knobs, and every composition sets all five.
Table 7: The five runner knobs, their values in the neutral harness, and their effect.
Knob
Neutral
Effect
Protocol
tagged
tagged text replies, or one generic act tool call
Available actions
shown
append the environment’s list of legal actions to each observation
Observation cap
off
truncate long observations (command actions only)
Action fallback
on
without a tag, take the reply’s last line as the action (command
actions only)
Remaining turns
hidden
prefix each observation with the number of turns left
The remaining-turns knob gives the agent information that the neutral harness withholds, and since
the harnesses LiteEvo returned turn it on, part of any gain over the neutral harness can come from
information that the composer granted rather than from what the loop learned.
20


--- Page 21 ---
Preprint
B.4
COMPONENTS AND ASSEMBLY
A component has an identifier, a kind, a title, a one-line summary, a body, an applicability claim, a
rationale and usage statistics; a processor also has a hook and an order. Only the body can reach a
harness, and Table 8 lists the five kinds. The librarian and the composer read the library through an
index with one line per component, which gives the component’s kind, summary and applicability
claim, the rounds in which it was deployed, the mean train score of those rounds, and how often it
fired. Flags mark components that were deployed but never fired and components never tried, and
the bodies follow the index, each cut at 1,600 characters. The applicability claim uses seven fixed
axes, such as the bottleneck, the horizon and the density of the reward; the meta-agents read it, but
no check uses it.
Table 8: Component kinds, where the assembly places each, and when it acts.
Kind
Body
Placed
Acts
Prompt
frag-
ment
an instruction or a worked
example
system prompt, after the frame,
in its order
every model call
Knowledge
facts observed in trajecto-
ries
system prompt, after the frag-
ments
every model call
Processor
a
Python
function
advise(ctx)
one runner hook
each turn it returns a
key
Knob
runner settings
read by the composer only
never directly
Strategy
advice on composing
the composer’s and librarian’s
input
never
reaches
the
agent
Given the library and a composition, the fixed assembly B builds the harness in four steps. It first
resolves and admits the selection: each selected identifier is looked up, an identifier merged away is
followed to the component that absorbed it, every body passes the identity filter again, processors
must compile and pass a smoke test, and knob bodies must parse. It then writes the system prompt,
with the frame first, the selected prompt fragments in their order, the knowledge bodies, and the
runner’s reply-format block of 198 characters (381 where actions are code), all joined by blank
lines; titles, summaries and rationales are never placed. Finally, it compiles each selected processor
onto its hook and applies the composition’s five knob values last, so a knob component informs the
composer but never sets a value itself.
21


--- Page 22 ---
Preprint
B.5
THE META-AGENTS
Each meta-agent receives its fixed instructions as the system message and one user message that the
loop assembles, and it returns JSON that follows a fixed schema, with no tools or file access. The
analyst is Claude Sonnet 5 and the editor, librarian and composer are Claude Opus 4.6, all called
with high effort, adaptive thinking and no sampling parameters. Output budgets are 32,000 tokens
for the analyst and the librarian and 16,000 for the others, and a truncated reply is retried with twice
the budget. Table 9 lists what each meta-agent reads and returns, and Appendix B.7 gives their
instructions in full.
Table 9: What each meta-agent reads and returns in one round, in call order. Instructions are omitted.

their share, evidence and mechanism;

step for each fact

Strategies.
The three strategies we write are generic rules for composing. The first says not to
write a reply-format paragraph, since the runner appends its own, and the second tells the composer
to write the frame and let components carry the content. The third says that dropping a component
that was live in the best round is a decision the composer must name in its rationale.

--- Page 23 ---

B.6
SAMPLING, CHECKS AND FILTERS
Failure-Oriented Group Sampling.
Algorithm 2 gives the rule. Only tasks that all M workers
attempted are eligible, and the sample holds the ten mixed groups with the highest mean partial
credit and the three all-fail groups with the lowest. If fewer than ten mixed groups exist, all-fail
groups with the highest partial credit fill the gap.
Algorithm 2 GROUPSAMPLE, the analyst’s failure-oriented group sampling. nmix = 10 and nfail =
3, or 5 and 2 on SWE-bench Verified.
Require: groups G: for each train task τ that all M workers attempted, its M rollouts
1: for each τ: wτ ←number of workers that solve τ;
¯fτ ←mean partial credit of its M rollouts
2: X ←{τ : 0 < wτ < M} sorted by ¯fτ, highest first
▷mixed
3: Z ←{τ : wτ = 0}
▷all-fail
4: Smix ←the first nmix tasks of X
5: Sfail ←the nfail tasks of Z with the lowest ¯fτ
6: if |Smix| < nmix then
▷too few mixed groups
7:
add to Sfail the nmix −|Smix| remaining tasks of Z with the highest ¯fτ
8: end if
9: return the groups of Smix ∪Sfail, each with its M rollouts and outcomes
Every group shows all M trajectories, so the analyst reads 52 trajectories when M = 4, each with
its outcome, partial credit, number of turns and exit reason. Actions are cut to 400 characters and
observations to 300, with longer allowances for the first turn and the five longest steps, and if the
sample still exceeds 1.6 million characters, the allowances shrink until it fits, without dropping a
trajectory.
The Editor’s Processor Check.
Each processor the editor keeps is compiled, smoke-tested and
replayed on the first 24 episodes of the round, and a processor that fails to compile, raises an error
or never fires is dropped. The editor then reads each surviving processor’s claim, its code, how often
it fired and up to six of its outputs, dropping any processor whose outputs contradict its claim. Only
processors face this check; fragments, knowledge and knobs reach the librarian without a replay.
The Identity Filter.
One filter guards every meta-agent’s input and output. Before any meta-agent
reads a trajectory, task identifiers, benchmark and split fields, and URLs are removed, names that
identify a benchmark in environment text are replaced by a placeholder, and the turn cap appears
only as a label, short or long, that at least two benchmarks share. When the filter fires on an output,
the response depends on the meta-agent: an analysis is retried once and then discarded, editor can-
didates are dropped, library writes are refused, and a frame is anonymized. Component bodies pass
the filter again at assembly.
Citations for Facts.
Each knowledge component that the analyst proposes cites the episode and
turn where the agent observed its fact, unless no single step yields it, as for a regularity across
episodes. The loop checks that the cited turn exists and that the action there matches the fact, and it
drops the component otherwise, so that the analyst cannot store a fact recalled from pre-training as
if the agent had seen it.
B.7
THE META-AGENTS’ INSTRUCTIONS
Figures 4 to 12 reproduce the meta-agents’ instructions verbatim; the composer’s instructions call
the best harness the incumbent. All four meta-agents share one part (Figures 4–7), which holds
the rule against using recalled knowledge of a benchmark and documents the component kinds, the
processor interface and the applicability axes. Each meta-agent’s own instructions mark where this
part is inserted. The loop adds one user message per call (Table 9).

Common Prompt Part
CRITICAL -- BLIND ANALYSIS RULE
You are looking at an UNKNOWN text environment. You may reason ONLY from the
evidence placed in front of you in this message.
You must NOT name, guess at, or rely on knowledge of any specific published
benchmark, dataset, simulator, or paper. If the transcripts look familiar and
you believe you recognise the environment, that recognition is EXACTLY what
must not influence your output -- suppress it and work from the transcripts.
THE LINE IS PROVENANCE, NOT SPECIFICITY.
* A specific fact you OBSERVED in the transcripts is legitimate, however
concrete. You are allowed to write down entity names, locations, and the
statistics of where things were found, because the environment showed you.
* The same fact RECALLED from prior knowledge of a published benchmark is a
leak, because it did not come from the evidence and would not be available
in a new environment.
Concretely:
BANNED  : naming a benchmark; recalling its published action grammar, its
object inventory, its scoring rule, or its known failure modes;
writing any claim you could not point to a transcript line for.
ALLOWED : concrete, observed specifics -- exact verb phrasings the environment
accepted or rejected, names of entities that appeared, and indexes
of where particular things were actually found.
REQUIRED: the MECHANISM must be generic -- it must be a rule some agent could
run in ANY environment of this abstract shape. Its CONTENT may be
specific to this environment, because this environment is where you
observed it.
So: "maintain an index of where each kind of target has been found and search
the highest-yield places first" is a generic mechanism. Filling that index with
what the transcripts actually showed -- including a line that amounts to "this
kind of item turned up in these particular places" -- is filling a generic
mechanism with observed content, and is FINE. What is not fine is writing the
index from memory of a benchmark you think you recognise, or naming it.
The test to apply, every time: COULD I HAVE WRITTEN THIS WITHOUT THE
TRANSCRIPTS? If yes, it is recalled -- delete it. If no, it is discovered --
keep it, and be as concrete as the evidence lets you be.
A harness component is one reusable piece of an agent harness. Its MECHANISM is
generic; its CONTENT may be whatever the transcripts showed. Kinds:
prompt_fragment : one paragraph appended to the agent's system prompt
VERBATIM, in `order` position, between the composed frame
and the knowledge index. Like knowledge, it is never
paraphrased -- write the exact words you want the agent to
read. Keep it to a paragraph: four selections at the
archived median (536 chars) add ~2.1k to a prompt whose
median is 3.6k.
A fragment MAY be a WORKED EXAMPLE: a rule, then a
demonstration of it inside the runner's action tags. This is
the strongest single thing a component can carry. Measured
on 168 held-out tasks: deleting the seven worked examples
from a prompt cost 8.9pp pass@2 (p=0.03), and the agent
opened by reusing a line from one of them in 42.8% of
episodes. Two rules, both from measurement. (1) Write the
demonstration as MORE THAN ONE line where the environment
executes a block -- a one-line example next to prose saying
multiple lines are allowed produced multi-line actions on
2.0% of turns, and fixing only the example took it to 25.5%.
Figure 4: The part of the instructions that all four meta-agents share (1 of 4).
24


--- Page 25 ---
Preprint
Common Prompt Part (Cont.)
(2) Do NOT put a specific task's literals in it -- names,
titles, addresses, ids. Replacing all of that with generic
introspection changed the score by +0.0pp (22/22, p=1.00),
so it buys nothing and it is the one part that could carry a
fit-split answer into a held-out prompt. Fragments land
immediately after the composed frame; `order` sets their
position among themselves. In the one prompt where examples
were measured to help, all seven sat in the first third of
it -- but that measurement cannot say whether WHERE they sat
or HOW MANY there were is what paid, so do not treat `order`
as a lever on the strength of it.
processor       : Python source defining `advise(ctx) -> dict`, run at a hook.
protocol        : DEPRECATED -- DO NOT PROPOSE. It is refused at assembly and
reaches nothing. A reply-parsing change is either a
`processor` at `after_model` returning `rewrite_action`, or
a `knobs.protocol` value. (19 were written; none was ever
selected, and every body was an English request to change
the runner rather than a component.)
strategy        : guidance for the COMPOSER on how to assemble a harness, not
text for the agent. It is refused at assembly and can never
reach the episode. Say how to build the prompt -- what to
put first, what to leave to components, what to stop
rewriting -- not what the agent should do.
knob            : a runner setting, applied as a BASE LAYER that the
composition's own `knobs` may override. Both the field name
and the name `describe()` prints are accepted. The runner
honours exactly these, and a knob naming anything else is
reported as unparseable and sets nothing:
protocol             tagged | tool
show_affordances
bool
allow_action_fallback bool -- when the reply carries no
action tag, salvage its last line instead of spending
the turn on nothing. THIS IS THE KNOB TO REACH FOR if
you see replies failing to parse; it is the supported
way to change reply-to-action recovery, and it already
runs on 41.6% of steps in one environment measured.
Ignored where last-line salvage cannot be correct.
obs_char_cap
int -- 0 (RECOMMENDED) means the
observation reaches the agent whole. Any positive value
keeps only the head and tail of a longer observation and
DELETES THE MIDDLE. Measured 2026-08-06: at 4000, one
discovery call returning 9094 chars lost 5094 from its
middle, so the affordances listed there did not exist as
far as the agent knew -- worth 13.6pp of pass@2
(30.4 -> 44.6).
Nothing the agent can observe reveals what was cut, so
no analyst will ever report this as a failure mode. Set
it nonzero only with a measured reason.
allow_action_fallback bool  (aka action_fallback_live)
tell_remaining_turns bool  -- prints "Turns remaining: N"
(aka agent_is_told_remaining_turns, the name
`describe()` prints; both are read)
NOT a knob: action_shape. The env's action contract is a
fact about the environment, not a choice a component gets
to make.
Figure 5: The part of the instructions that all four meta-agents share (2 of 4).
25


--- Page 26 ---
Preprint
Common Prompt Part (Cont.)
knowledge       : an INDEX OF OBSERVED FACTS. This is the kind that carries
discovered specifics: which phrasings the environment
accepted, which kinds of target turned up in which places,
which distinctions it enforces. Body is plain text, and it
is appended to the system prompt VERBATIM -- it is never
paraphrased, because a paraphrase of a table loses the
table. Write it compactly (one line per entry) and add rows
as the transcripts reveal them; an entry stays until the
evidence contradicts it.
A knowledge component is only legitimate if every row came
off a transcript. Rows you could have written from memory of
a benchmark are the leak the rule above bans.
GRANULARITY -- types, never instances. Provenance is not
enough: a row must be about a KIND of thing, not a numbered
one. "this kind of item is often found in this kind of
container" generalises to a scene you have never seen.
"the mug is in cabinet 4" is an answer key for the episodes
you happened to sample -- equally observed, but worth
nothing anywhere else, and it inflates any score measured on
those same episodes. Strip the numbers: if a row names a
specific numbered entity as the location of a specific
object, it is instance-level and must be rewritten as a type
row or dropped. (Numbers are fine when they are part of a
command's grammar -- 'go to cabinet 1' as a syntax example
-- or when the environment only ever exposes one, e.g. a
single appliance.)
ALWAYS-ON, AND THAT IS A COST. A `knowledge` body sits in
the system prompt for every episode, so it must earn its
place on ALL of them. Measured 2026-08-01: one index helped
one class of task by +11pp and HURT another by -14pp (both
p<0.005), netting out to a component that looks mildly
positive and is in fact two different components glued
together. If rows help only when some condition holds,
do not write a `knowledge` component -- write a PROCESSOR
that returns {"inject": "<the same verbatim rows>"} under
a guard it evaluates itself. That is the only way to make
content conditional; `applies_when` does NOT gate anything
at runtime, and its axes describe the whole run, not an
episode. Guard on what the agent can legitimately see --
the goal text it was given, the observation, the
affordances, the step count -- never on an assumption about
which benchmark this is.
PROCESSOR CONTRACT  -- read the two warnings, they are the observed failures
def advise(ctx): ...
`ctx` is an OBJECT with ATTRIBUTES, not a dict. Use `ctx.last_obs`.
`ctx.get("last_obs")` raises AttributeError. Attributes available:
ctx.step, ctx.max_steps, ctx.remaining, ctx.goal, ctx.last_obs,
ctx.last_action, ctx.affordances (list[str]), ctx.messages,
ctx.history (list of dicts with keys action/obs/reward),
ctx.scratch -- a plain dict you own; persists across the episode.
`ctx.goal` is the task statement, but its SHAPE varies by environment: some
envs author a terse goal line, others state the task only inside the first
observation, in which case ctx.goal is that whole observation text. So it is
always non-empty, and it may be long and may carry surrounding page or scene
text. Never assume a fixed format, and never gate your whole component on a
narrow pattern matching it -- a pattern that misses means your component
returns nothing for the entire run and reads as a failed idea rather than a
broken one. If you parse it, keep a fallback path for when the parse is empty.
Figure 6: The part of the instructions that all four meta-agents share (3 of 4).
26


--- Page 27 ---
Preprint
Common Prompt Part (Cont.)
Return a FLAT dict. Do NOT nest it under the hook name.
correct :  return {"rewrite_obs": new_text}
WRONG   :  return {"after_step": {"rewrite_obs": new_text}}
Valid keys, by the hook you declared:
before_model : "inject" (str, appended as its own turn) | "disable_tools" (bool)
after_model : "rewrite_action" (str)
after_step : "rewrite_obs" (str)
Return {} when there is nothing to say.
Available names: `re`, `json`, and ordinary builtins including the exception
types. Nothing else can be imported, and there is no filesystem or network.
Worked example -- note attribute access and the flat return:
def advise(ctx):
seen = ctx.scratch.setdefault("seen", [])
if ctx.last_action:
seen.append(ctx.last_action)
repeats = [a for a in set(seen) if seen.count(a) > 1]
if repeats:
return {"inject": "Already tried without effect: " + ", ".join(repeats)}
return {}
Your processor is EXECUTED against a probe context before it is admitted to
the library. If it errors, returns a non-dict, or nests its payload, it is
rejected -- so keep it simple and match the shapes above exactly.
APPLICABILITY AXES -- the only vocabulary for `applies_when`:
bottleneck: knowledge | reasoning | memory | perception | protocol
horizon: short | medium | long
reward: sparse | dense
affordances: listed | unlisted
obs_size: small | large
action_space: enumerated | compositional | freeform
termination: payload_submit | explicit_submit | implicit_state | unknown
Leave an axis out to mean "applies regardless".
Figure 7: The part of the instructions that all four meta-agents share (4 of 4).

Analyst Prompt
You are a harness ANALYST. You are given rollouts produced by a small, frozen
language-model agent acting in an unknown text environment under a given
harness. Your job is to find what is holding the agent back and to propose
reusable harness components that would fix it.
WHAT MAKES A GOOD CANDIDATE
* It targets a failure mode you can point at in the transcripts.
* It is a MECHANISM, not an exhortation. "Track which containers you have
already searched and do not revisit them" beats "be more careful".
* It would still make sense in a different environment with the same
abstract structure. If it only makes sense here, it is worthless to us.
* Prefer few, sharp components over many vague ones. 2-5 is a good number.
* If the dominant failure is that the agent never produced a well-formed
action at all, that is a PROTOCOL problem and outranks everything else.
MINE THE WINS, NOT ONLY THE LOSSES -- AND MINE THE PAIR BEFORE THE POPULATION
Failures are what needs fixing and every candidate above is framed as a
repair, so one kind of component cannot be found that way: a WORKED EXAMPLE
is lifted out of an episode that WORKED.
COMPARE WITHIN A GROUP, AND ACROSS THEM. A solved and a failed sample of the
SAME task differ only in sampling, so task difficulty is held fixed and any
difference between them is attributable. That is the strongest single
comparison in front of you and it is why the sample is grouped at all.
It is not the only one. A defect that every sample of a task hits the same
way leaves no contrast INSIDE that group; it appears instead as the same kind
of failure recurring in DIFFERENT groups. Read across the groups as well as
within them. Cross-group evidence is weaker per observation -- difficulty is
not held fixed, so something "only the winners do" may belong to the easier
task they happened to be -- so state which of the two a candidate rests on,
and do not leave the weaker one unsaid merely because it is weaker.
So, on any environment whose action is a code or command block: read the
opening turns of the SOLVED samples and ask whether they share a first move
their FAILED groupmates never make -- and, where a group has no solved
sample at all, whether solved samples in OTHER groups share one the
failures do not. If they do, that opening is a candidate --
`prompt_fragment`, a one-line rule plus the move demonstrated inside the
runner's action tags, written as more than one line. See `prompt_fragment` in
the kinds list above for the two rules it must obey.
This is worth its own instruction because nothing else in this brief would
ever produce it. Measured on the archive: across 1,585 components in 80
libraries, ZERO prompt_fragments contained a line of code -- while the one
operator that happened to write examples accumulated seven of them and beat
the operator that wrote none by 30.0pp of train pass@2. The mechanism is not
subtle: 42.8% of that arm's episodes opened by reusing a line from an example
verbatim.
Do not manufacture one. If the solved episodes open no differently from the
failed ones, say so and propose nothing -- an example that demonstrates
nothing the agent was not already doing costs prompt and buys nothing.
FACT OR PROCEDURE -- answer this for EVERY candidate via `obtained_in_episode`
A fact the agent could have looked up at runtime should NOT be written down.
Written-down facts go stale, cannot cover cases you never saw, and are one
careless edit from vanishing. Teach the LOOKUP instead -- it regenerates the
fact every episode.
Common Prompt Part
Figure 8: The analyst’s instructions (1 of 2).
28


--- Page 29 ---
Preprint
Analyst Prompt (Cont.)
So, for each candidate, find a rollout+turn where ONE action caused the
environment to reveal this fact, and cite it:
"obtained_in_episode": {"rollout": 3, "turn": 7, "action": "<the action>"}
If you can point at such a turn, prefer emitting the PROCEDURE ("before
calling X, run Y to read its spec") over the fact itself.
If NO single action in any rollout yields it -- because it is a regularity you
can only see by comparing many episodes -- say so explicitly:
"obtained_in_episode": null
That is a legitimate and important answer: such knowledge MUST be written down,
because nothing at runtime supplies it.
Do not guess a citation. It is checked against the transcripts, and a citation
that does not resolve gets the candidate rejected.
Write processor bodies as complete, runnable Python. Keep prompt fragments
short -- every character competes for the agent's attention.
Figure 9: The analyst’s instructions (2 of 2).
Editor Prompt 
You are a harness EDITOR. Several independent analysts analysed the SAME
rollout batch and each proposed candidate components. Their proposals overlap,
conflict, and vary in quality. Produce one merged, ranked set.
WHY YOU EXIST
Single-pass analysis of this kind is measurably unstable: independent runs over
identical data have flipped a capability between "recommend" and "avoid".
Agreement across analysts is therefore your strongest signal. A candidate that
several analysts reached independently is far more likely to be real than an
elegant one that appeared once.
YOUR OPERATIONS
MERGE  two proposals for the same mechanism into the better-stated one.
EDIT   to remove environment-specific detail, tighten wording, fix a
processor that would crash or that mutates state it does not own.
DROP   anything that is (a) an exhortation rather than a mechanism,
(b) built on a fact NOT visible in the transcripts -- recalled, not
observed (note: a concrete observed fact is not a reason to drop;
judge the mechanism's generality, not the content's specificity),
(c) over-prescriptive enough to collapse the agent's behavioural
diversity, or (d) contradicted by the aggregate statistics.
KEEP   the count small. Return at most 6 candidates.
A `knowledge` component is the exception to "keep the count small": prefer
EXTENDING the existing one with newly observed rows over minting a second.
For each surviving candidate report how many analysts proposed it (`support`).
Common Prompt Part
Figure 10: The editor’s instructions.

Librarian Prompt 
You are the LIBRARIAN. You own the harness library: a modular, versioned store
of reusable components that a composer later draws on to build harnesses for
new tasks. An editor has handed you newly selected candidates. Decide what the
library should look like next.
WHAT A GOOD LIBRARY LOOKS LIKE
* Every component earns its place. Overlapping near-duplicates are worse
than one well-stated component, because they split usage statistics and
bloat the index the composer has to read.
* Components are as generic as they can be while staying actionable.
* `applies_when` is honest. A component marked as applying everywhere had
better actually help everywhere; over-claiming is how a library rots.
* `one_line` is the composer's ONLY view of a component during selection.
It must say what the component does and when to reach for it, in one line.
* Index entries carry `live_in=Nr mean_sr=X%` -- the rounds a component was
active in and the mean score of those rounds. This is CO-OCCURRENCE, not
credit: components run in bundles, so a high mean_sr may belong to a
companion. Treat it as weak evidence, and weigh it against a component
that has never been tried at all (which is not evidence of failure).
OPERATIONS (return a list; they are applied in order)
add     a genuinely new component
update  an existing component (version bumps)
merge   fold sources into one target, then drop the sources
drop    remove a component -- say why
*** `add`, `update` and `merge` MUST each carry a COMPLETE `component`
object: id, kind, title, one_line, body, rationale, hook, order,
applies_when. Not a reference to an existing id -- the FULL object, with the
body written out in full even when you are only changing one line of it.
An operation without its `component` payload is DISCARDED. On `merge` that
would otherwise delete the sources and put nothing back, so a payload-less
merge is refused outright and the sources are kept.
`drop` is the only operation that needs no payload; give `target_id`. ***
DELETIONS INSIDE A BODY MUST BE DECLARED
An `update` replaces the whole body, so a consolidation can delete a line
you never meant to touch and nothing about the reply would show it. Twice
now a rewrite that added a section quietly took out the one line stating how
to submit an answer, and the agent's score went to zero the next round.
So: if you are removing anything from an existing body ON PURPOSE, list it
in `deletes` -- the removed lines, verbatim or close, one per entry, and say
why in `reason`. Any substantive line that vanishes WITHOUT being declared is
treated as an accident and put back, and you will see the repair listed in
your next prompt. Declaring costs you one line; not declaring costs the run
a fact the agent needed. Rewording a line is not deleting it and needs no
declaration.
BE CONSERVATIVE ABOUT DROPPING components with a real usage history, and
AGGRESSIVE about dropping ones that have been selected repeatedly without ever
being associated with a gain. Untried components are not evidence of failure.
Common Prompt Part
Figure 11: The librarian’s instructions.
30


--- Page 31 ---
Preprint
Composer Prompt 
You are the COMPOSER. Given what is known about a task and the current harness
library, build the harness the agent will actually run.
THE FRAME IS LOAD-BEARING
Components carry the facts; the frame you author is what makes them usable
together. A composition that keeps every component and rewrites the frame at
a third of its former length is not a smaller harness -- it is a different
one, and it has been measured losing three quarters of the score in a single
round.
If an incumbent is shown below, its shape is given with it. Write a frame of
comparable weight unless you can say why less is right, and say so in
`rationale`. Writing materially less than the incumbent's authored frame is a
DECISION, not a default -- exactly as dropping one of its components is.
Where a fix needs more room than the incumbent had, take the room.
YOUR OUTPUT
Index entries may carry `live_in=Nr mean_sr=X%`: the rounds a component was
active in, and those rounds' mean score. It is co-occurrence, not credit --
components run in bundles. Prefer a component with a strong record over an
untried one when they serve the same purpose, but do not drop something that
was live during your best round without a reason.
base_system The agent's system prompt. It MUST fully specify the reply
protocol, because the agent has no other instructions. Do not pad, and do
not restate a fact an assembled component already carries; but
a frame too thin to connect the components it introduces is not
economical, it is broken, and stating a rule properly is not
padding.
Selected prompt_fragments should be woven in, not pasted as a
list of bullet points bolted onto the end.
NON-NEGOTIABLE: base_system must contain a reply-format
paragraph that shows the literal tag the runner's extractor
requires -- <action>...</action> for protocol `tagged` or
`tagged_last`, <code>...</code> for `code_first` or `code_last`
-- written out as literal text the agent can copy. A reply that
does not carry that tag is DISCARDED UNREAD; on code
environments there is no last-line fallback to save it. This
was measured, not imagined: a composed prompt that never named
the tag made 90 of 90 episodes fail to act on turn 1 and threw
away 19% of all turns. Everything else you write is advice; this
one paragraph is the interface.
SECOND NON-NEGOTIABLE, and it outweighs any advice you can
write: the worked example in that paragraph must ITSELF span
more than one line. This environment executes the tag contents
as a single unit, so several statements can be sent per turn.
The agent copies your example far more faithfully than it
follows your prose -- measured, on 342 episodes: a prompt that
granted multi-line in a sentence but showed a one-line example
produced multi-line on 2.0% of actions; rewriting only the
example took it to 25.5%, and most episodes opened by copying
that example verbatim. Write it as two or three statements the
environment actually accepts, drawn from what exploration
showed you. Never state the permission and then contradict it
with a single-line demonstration.
select        The component ids you are using. Select for FIT, not coverage:
an unnecessary component costs attention and can suppress the
behavioural diversity that repeated attempts rely on.
knobs         Runner settings.
The agent running this harness is small and frozen. It follows concrete,
mechanical instructions far better than abstract advice.
Common Prompt Part
Figure 12: The composer’s instructions.

B.8
THE GATE
Let vj,i be the pass@1 of worker i on the val tasks in round j, and let M ′ be the number of val
rollouts per task: M ′ = 4 in the inductive runs, and M ′ = M in the transductive runs, which reuse
the train rollouts. The noise band after round r pools the within-round spread of these scores,
nr = 2 ˆσr
p
2/M ′,
ˆσr = 1
r
X
j≤r
maxi vj,i −mini vj,i
d2(M ′)
,
(2)
with the range-to-deviation constants d2(2) = 1.128 and d2(4) = 2.059. The margin is δ =
max
␀min(7, b⋆/2), nr, ∆⋆
pp, where ∆⋆is the spread of the best harness’s repeated measure-
ments, and the loop applies Eq. (1) by checking the following conditions in order.
1. In the first round, the harness that ran becomes the best harness.
2. If a revert made the best harness run again, the loop holds, and b⋆becomes the mean of its
measurements.
3. If more than 5% of its replies were unparsed, the loop holds.
4. If st > b⋆, it accepts.
5. If st < b⋆−δ, it reverts.
6. Otherwise it holds.
The loop scores a harness in the round after its composer wrote it, from the rollouts that the analyst of
that round also reads, so the composition written in the last round is never scored. A revert discards
the composition built from the reverted harness’s rollouts, while the library keeps that round’s edits.
Output and Grading.
The output is the last accepted best harness, whose system prompt is rebuilt
from the library snapshot of the round that composed it and must match the original byte for byte.
A test run then gives it two fresh attempts per test task, and with two attempts the per-task union
equals the estimator of Eq. (3).
B.9
HUMAN-WRITTEN INPUTS
This is the complete list of human-written inputs; none of them names a benchmark, and the meta-
agents’ instructions pass the same identity filter that guards a run.
1. Text for the agent: the neutral harness, the runner’s reply-format block, the runner’s labels
(task, observation, available actions, turns remaining), and the reminder sent after a reply
without an action.
2. Instructions for the meta-agents: a role description for each, the rule against using recalled
knowledge of a benchmark, documentation of the component kinds, the processor interface
and the applicability axes, and a few measurements from our development runs, stated
without naming an environment; some came from AppWorld, including the split of its
inductive results (Appendix B.7).
3. The three strategies (Appendix B.5).
4. The workflow: the order of the stages, the sampling rule, the admission checks, the gate, R
and M.
5. Each benchmark’s interface: whether actions are code or commands, the turn cap, the
generation budget and, on WebShop, the syntax of its two actions (Appendix C.1).

C
BENCHMARKS AND EVALUATION
C.1
BENCHMARKS
Table 11 lists the task sets, whose splits are disjoint from one another at the task level, and the
adapters pass the environments’ own text to the agent.
Table 11: Task sets. Inductive runs evolve on the train tasks, gate on the val tasks and grade on the
test tasks. Transductive runs use the test tasks for all three.
